entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Raḍwān ibn Muḥammad al-Sāʻātī, a Syrian Muslim physician, government official, and writer, was a key figure in the 13th-century Islamic Golden Age. Born in the Khurāsān region of present-day Uzbekistan, al-Sāʻātī traveled extensively throughout the Middle East, serving as a physician and advisor to various rulers.

He is best known for his contributions to the field of medicine, particularly in the development of medical practices and treatments for various diseases. His works, such as the 'Kitāb al-Ṭibb' (Book of Medicine), remain influential to this day.

Al-Sāʻātī's legacy extends beyond his medical contributions, as he was also a prominent figure in the cultural and intellectual life of the Islamic world during this period. His writings and translations helped spread knowledge and ideas across the region.

In 1230, al-Sāʻātī passed away in Damascus, leaving behind a significant impact on the development of medicine and Islamic culture. His work continues to be studied and celebrated by scholars and medical professionals around the world.

Raḍwān ibn Muḥammad al-Sāʻātī's life and achievements serve as a testament to the enduring power of knowledge and intellectual exchange during the Islamic Golden Age.

entities.summary: Fakhr al-Dīn Riḍwān ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Rustam al-Khurāsānī al-Sāʿātī, known as Ibn al-Sāʿātī, was a Syrian Muslim physician, government official, and writer who lived in the 13th century. Born in 1195 in Damascus, Syria, he studied medicine under the renowned physician Ibn Rushd in Cordoba, Spain, where he was exposed to the latest scientific and philosophical ideas. Ibn al-Sāʿātī’s works on medicine and astronomy were widely respected in his time, and he was appointed as a government official in the Khwarezmid Empire, where he played a key role in promoting Islamic education and culture. He died in 1230 in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, leaving behind a legacy of scholarship and intellectual curiosity that continues to inspire historians and scholars today.
